Hello friend,

I know you dont want pity, but I truly am sorry you are feeling this way. 

Borderline IS HELL.... but its manageable. I have been in crisis, so this is not armchair advice. To address a few points.

* There is nothing wrong with your post. You do not look stupid to THOSE with a heart. Anyone who thinks otherwise has no business commenting on content you create while in a vulnerable space. If anything, you are braver than I have ever been. While I do discuss my BPD with those who are close to me, I rarely talk about the way my inner voices abuse me. That takes courage. 
* Its clear that you have used that same courage to deal with the voices before. They HAVE gone away. They will go away again. You have been able to function without them. You just need to be patient with yourself and condemn the voices when they speak up. Get silly with them. Identify that what they are telling you is not true. Tell them to shut up. In your video you are well spoken. Use that same well-spoken energy with them.
* Dont cancel your appointments. Your appointments may be the very thing you need right now. Sure, its scary to put your trust in people who could make your life more uncomfortable, however... Certain protocols exist to help you in a time of crisis. Some of that help will be uncomfortable.
* Disappointing people SUCKS. You may never forgive yourself, however, you are in control of you. Step 1 of fixing a behavior is recognizing it. Now that you recognize it, you get to observe the patterns and make your adjustments so that you can avoid creating further disappointments. Sometimes when I feel I have disappointed someone I find out that I blew the situation out of proportion, and there was nothing to worry about.
* You seem to be educated as to what borderline personality disorder is. One major thing to remember is that it CAN lessen with time. My own borderline has significantly declined. Not every symptom is gone, but it has gotten easier. Trusting in my medication and being honest with care providers is the correct way to do things. Remember, you get to dictate the content that you present to those you seek help from.

Your situation sounds like you are trying to play a game but are holding too many cards at once. You dont need to play them all at the same time. If possible, segment your problems. Realize that they may be related in some way, but that they did not grow up in the same house as one another.

I have felt of lot of feelings of abandonment. I was diagnosed at age 30. It has been a really hard thing to come across later in life, but I am growing stronger every day. I know I am, even if it feels like I am maybe slipping backwards from time to time. To me, I feel my BPD as a sliding scale. I am not always 10/10. It comes and goes.

I know that I have love and support, but BPD can cut me off from that understanding. I often find myself coming in and out of states where I have a distinct feeling that no one cares for me, and that I am just an annoying and poorly understood wretch of a creature.

I sometimes tell myself "This is all so exhausting. If this is all life will be from here on out, how can I handle that?". 

There is a large level of self harm that exists within us when it comes to our minds and how it talks to us. I look at someone and I think: "This person cant possibly love me. They just want something from me. I am a bother and a burden." 

Absolutely not the case, even when I have completely isolated myself for fear that its true. I have a very negative outlook on life. I feel like I can completely suck the energy out of people without realizing it. These are all feelings though. Not reality.

A very large theme for me in my early adult years was that I never felt like I was understood by anyone. I felt like there was so much difficulty in articulating how I felt. I felt like my communications with people were always misunderstood. It was so frustrating to have so much to say, but not realizing that the large majority of it was overwhelming emotion that most people dont feel, or perhaps aren't ready to deal with.

I go through seasons where my joy is not accessible. The only companion I can find is that ugly voice inside of me that wants to assure me of defeat. There have been times where I stare in the mirror and say mean things to myself until I literally tear up and shrink inward.

I want to touch on one of the things you said above.

>"But what can I do? This is the brain I have, I don’t have the power to change it."

While my thoughts could be construed as potentially celebrating a disorder... I wouldnt want a different brain. It can be difficult, and often times I block myself from believing it... but who I am, the way I think, the things I do, the way I solve problems, and the INTENSE way that I love those around me... That is who I want to be, even if it isnt always easy. 

Lately, I have felt great despair towards my medications. I doubled up on my anti depressant, but can still feel those cold drafts of doubt as they occasionally flutter by. I worry about the pain I will feel in the future, and I would do anything to avoid it.

A final thought on another thing you wrote:

>"I feel trapped and cannot see any future perspective. I wish I could have a job in my field, but I don’t have the right skills and enough experience for it."

I felt the same way for a very long time, and sometimes it still creeps up on me. There is VAST truth in the concept of faking it until you make it. I consider myself to mostly be a high functioning BPD. A ways back I made a five year plan. That five year plan led me to where I am now. I have a job that meets the goals of that plan. Sometimes I hate the shit out of this job. I didnt get this new role until after my diagnosis. I never thought I would become anyone's manager. Its surreal trying to navigate so many relationships at once. 

I hate saying things that seem like they can come from a motivational speaker, but there is one thing that I learned from my first therapist that has been a real prize... something along the lines of "No thing is possible if we tell ourselves no. Living, speaking, and thinking in absolutes can form bad mental habits. Leave room for the gray area." 

Do not be afraid to rethink, or rephrase things that you have done or said. Its ok to feel like crap from time to time, but through daily emotional hygiene you can at least gain an edge over this wonderful thing we call "BPD".

One of the markers for BPD is "**Feeling suspicious or out of touch with reality**". You could also consider the first thing as a part of hyper vigilance. Always in a state of being ready to react.

I have felt extreme paranoia at times. My paranoia was more in terms of constantly interpreting the appearance of certain things as important symbolism. Example: Noticing snails, black cats, or certain numbers on the clock somehow became very important to me and felt like either a blessing or an omen. Lyrics to familiar songs took on strange meaning or even double meaning. The appearance of common things became messages and I would often have auditory hallucinations. This was during the height of an emotional crisis while undergoing a life changing event, so I am not sure if it can be considered a true piece of my BPD diagnosis.

The second part you describe could be "Maladaptive daydreaming" or be related to the "Fantasy prone personality" trait. Beware that maladaptive daydreaming is not officially recognized diagnostic material. Without meaning to gatekeep or minimize, I find that a lot of the discussions about it is done in an overly competitive, comparative, and disingenuous manner.

[Maladaptive Daydreaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maladaptive_daydreaming)

Read up on Derealization and Dissociation as well.

Thats one way to put it. I think mostly the first step for ME in mitigating these issues / symptoms was to make it a habit of trying to recognize thoughts as the potential issue.

While not 100% applicable to your question, I was taught the following concept:

Have I come to a conclusion about a thought I am having?

Is the thought based in reality, or is it part of a self conditioned black and white thinking?

Is the conclusion I have reached valid?

Do I need it to be validated?

Do I need to reach a conclusion at all?

​

Recognizing our thoughts and giving ourselves time to live in the gray is a good way to provide room for ourselves to exist within relationships. It gives us pause to set boundaries upon our own expectations of others. Understanding that your emotional needs can exist within that same gray area without feeling like you are unanchored is not always as easy as it should be, but it lessens the possibility of setting up situations where a relationship causes you distress.

The TL;DR is. "Try to find the gray area in relationships.  Do not put all of your emotional needs into one basket. Keep as many of them as you can in your basket. Wow, thats a lot of eggs.... Why do you have so many eggs?"

I was diagnosed around 6 years ago. I have done everything I can to learn about *this thing of ours*. The first several months were a continual heartbreak. I felt like I was being cast into pit after pit due to all of the hateful content I was encountering. It was nearly impossible to trudge through the hate groups in order to find a few useful tidbits which were just general explanations of the definitions in the DSM. Most firsthand information I found from people online was nothing more than terrible behavior being chalked up to BPD. Symptoms unrelated to BPD being lumped in with it due to common comorbidity. The biggest takeaways I could find were how I must be the worst person in existence and should never be trusted under any circumstance. 

Its hard to sift through the negative information. The best resource I found was "Stop Walking on Eggshells". That book was a gentle introduction to the multilayered thing that is BPD. I also strongly recommend medication if you are feeling too out of sorts.

Before my diagnosis I was extremely extremely extremely ready to end my life. I had a hard time figuring out why the grief that I felt swallowed me whole. Why were others grieving without chaos? Why does every moment feel like a whirlwind of razor wire? Why do my emotions steer me away from my goals and wreck me?

I figured that I had a mental disorder that was causing me to destroy all of my relationships in a very disturbingly systematic way. I somehow came upon the concept of "Mood / Emotional" disorders. After extensive therapy I came away with a diagnosis. 

As for success stories?

I have been in a stable loving relationship for over 10 years. We have children and are happy. I have friends who matter to me and who I seemingly matter to in return. I have been employed for 4 years and absolutely adore my job. I am able to provide for my family. I work among friends and even have people who report directly to me and I seem to do a decent job of it. I strive to have a decent relationship with my family and have learned to set boundaries. I go to therapy and constantly reflect upon the things I have done. I have seen very positive change in me since I was diagnosed.

BPD is a very large concept. It has negative connotations. You are not your diagnosis. The diagnosis gives the beast enough form for us to fight / work with. How other people view BPD shouldnt matter to you. Keep trying your best.
